Those qualities of mind commonly termed analytical are themselves scarcely open to analysis. We recognise them only through their results. Among other things, we know that, when possessed in unusual measure, they invariably afford their possessor the keenest enjoyment. Just as the strong man rejoices in his bodily powers, taking pleasure in exercises that bring his muscles into use, so the analyst delights in the mental activity that disentangles. Even the most insignificant employment of his gift yields him pleasure. He loves enigmas, conundrums, and hieroglyphics, displaying in his solution of each an acuteness that seems to ordinary understanding almost supernatural. His conclusions, attained through the very spirit and substance of method, nevertheless wear the complete appearance of intuition.

The power of resolution may be greatly strengthened by mathematical study, particularly by its highest branch, which has unfairly been named analysis, as though pre-eminently so, merely because its operations proceed backwards. But calculation does not of itself constitute analysis. A chess-player, for instance, performs the former without attempting the latter. The influence of chess upon mental character is consequently much misconceived. I am not composing a treatise here, but merely introducing a rather singular narrative with observations of a somewhat casual kind; I shall therefore venture to maintain that the loftier powers of reflective intelligence are exercised more thoroughly and more profitably by the unpretending game of draughts than by the whole elaborate trifling of chess. In the latter game, whose pieces have different and fantastic movements, and values both diverse and changing, mere complexity is confused with depth—an error by no means uncommon. Attention is brought into vigorous exercise. Should it slacken for a moment, a mistake occurs, bringing disadvantage or defeat. Since the possible moves are not merely numerous but intricate, the opportunities for such mistakes multiply; and in nine instances out of ten the victor is the player with greater concentration, rather than greater acuteness. In draughts, conversely, where the movements are uniform and admit little variety, the likelihood of an inadvertent mistake is lessened. Mere attention being thus comparatively idle, whatever advantage either player secures must arise from superior discernment. To put the matter less abstractly, suppose a game of draughts in which only four kings remain, and in which, naturally, no oversight is anticipated. It is plain that, with players at all evenly matched, success here can turn only upon some unusually subtle move, born of a powerful exertion of the understanding.

Mr. Merton was greatly upset when the wedding was postponed a second time. Lady Julia, who had already ordered her wedding dress, did everything she could to persuade Sybil to end the engagement. But although Sybil dearly loved her mother, she had entrusted her whole life to Lord Arthur. Nothing Lady Julia said could shake her faith in him. Lord Arthur himself needed several days to recover from his terrible disappointment, and for a while his nerves were completely shattered. Before long, however, his excellent common sense returned. His sensible, practical mind quickly settled what he should do next. Since poison had failed altogether, the obvious course was to try dynamite, or some other kind of explosive.

He therefore went through the list of his friends and relatives again. After careful thought, he decided to blow up his uncle, the Dean of Chichester. The Dean was a highly educated and cultured man with a great love of clocks. His remarkable collection ranged from fifteenth-century timepieces to modern ones. Lord Arthur thought this hobby offered an excellent chance to carry out his plan. Getting an explosive device was, of course, quite a different problem. The London Directory offered no help on that subject. He also felt there was little point in asking Scotland Yard, since they never seemed to know anything about the activities of the dynamite faction until an explosion had occurred, and knew very little even then.

Suddenly he remembered his friend Rouvaloff, a young Russian with strongly revolutionary views, whom he had met at Lady Windermere’s during the winter. Count Rouvaloff was said to be writing a biography of Peter the Great. He had supposedly come to England to study documents about the Tsar’s time in the country working as a ship’s carpenter. Most people suspected, however, that he was an agent of the Nihilist movement, and the Russian Embassy certainly disapproved of his presence in London. Lord Arthur felt that Rouvaloff was exactly the man he needed. One morning he drove to the Count’s rooms in Bloomsbury to ask for advice and help.

‘So you are beginning to take politics seriously?’ Count Rouvaloff asked after Lord Arthur explained the purpose of his visit. But Lord Arthur disliked any sort of boasting, and felt obliged to admit that he had no interest whatever in social questions. He wanted the explosive device only for a strictly family matter, which concerned nobody except himself.

Reading his letter again while she answered it softened Harriet’s feelings so much that she especially needed a few firm words to strengthen her resolve. She was deeply troubled at the thought of making him unhappy. She kept wondering what his mother and sisters would think and say, and was anxious that they should not consider her ungrateful. Emma believed that if the young man had appeared before Harriet just then, she would have accepted him after all.

Still, the letter was written, sealed, and sent. The matter was settled, and Harriet was safe. She remained rather sad throughout the evening, but Emma understood her kind-hearted regrets. Sometimes she eased them by speaking of her own affection for Harriet, and sometimes by bringing up Mr. Elton.

‘I shall never be asked to Abbey-Mill again,’ Harriet said in a rather mournful voice.

‘And even if you were, I could never bear to let you go, my Harriet. We need you far too much at Hartfield to spare you for Abbey-Mill.’

‘I am sure I should never wish to go there, either. I am only happy when I am at Hartfield.’

A little later she said, ‘I think Mrs. Goddard would be very surprised if she knew what had happened. Miss Nash certainly would. Miss Nash thinks her own sister has married very well, and her husband is only a linen seller.’

‘We should hardly wish a schoolteacher to have greater pride or more refined tastes, Harriet. I expect Miss Nash would envy you such a chance to marry. Even winning this man’s affection would seem valuable to her. I suppose she knows nothing of your chances of something better. A certain person’s attentions can scarcely have become part of Highbury gossip yet. So far, I imagine you and I are the only people who have understood the meaning of his looks and behaviour.’

Harriet blushed and smiled, and murmured something about being surprised that people liked her so much. Thinking of Mr. Elton certainly cheered her; but after a while her sympathy for the rejected Mr. Martin returned.

‘He has my letter by now,’ she said quietly. ‘I wonder what they are all doing—whether his sisters know. If he is unhappy, they will be unhappy too. I hope he will not take it too much to heart.’

‘Let us think of our absent friends who are enjoying themselves more,’ Emma exclaimed. ‘Perhaps at this very moment Mr. Elton is showing your picture to his mother and sisters. He is telling them how much prettier you are in person, and, after they have asked five or six times, letting them hear your name—your own dear name.’
